blogs.title: Before Day 5: When HIT Comes Early After Cardiac Surgery
blogs.description: This post explores the diagnostic challenge of early-onset HIT occurring before postoperative day 5, a timing that falls outside the classic HIT temporal window. Using the case as a framework, we review how preoperative heparin exposures—such as during cardiac catheterization—can 'pre-prime' the immune system, leading to a rapid platelet count decline upon re-exposure during surgery. We discuss why clinicians should routinely probe for recent preoperative heparin exposures when evaluating early postoperative thrombocytopenia, how this alters the pre-test probability of HIT, and how the classic '5-to-10-day' teaching can mislead if preoperative exposures are overlooked.

blogs.title: Autoimmune HIT: When Antibodies Don't Need Heparin to Cause Havoc
blogs.description: This post provides an overview of autoimmune HIT (aHIT), a recently recognized and increasingly important subtype of HIT in which antibodies activate platelets in a heparin-independent manner. We contrast classic HIT pathophysiology with aHIT, focusing on the serotonin-release assay (SRA) pattern of strong platelet activation even at 0 U/mL heparin. Using this case, we review the clinical features that suggest aHIT—profoundly low platelet nadirs, delayed or incomplete response to IVIG, consumptive coagulopathy with falling fibrinogen and rising D-dimer, and thrombosis despite therapeutic anticoagulation. We discuss why recognizing aHIT matters for prognosis and treatment selection, including the rationale for adding high-dose IVIG to anticoagulation.

blogs.title: The Indeterminate SRA: A Novel Serological Profile in Autoimmune HIT
blogs.description: This post dives into the laboratory diagnosis of HIT, using the case's unique SRA profile as a teaching vehicle. We review how the screening PF4/polyanion ELISA and confirmatory SRA are interpreted in routine HIT, and then unpack this patient's atypical findings: strong serotonin release at 0 U/mL heparin (indicating aHIT) combined with only partial inhibition by the Fc receptor-blocking monoclonal antibody IV.3—a profile never previously reported. We discuss how such atypical laboratory results can lead to an 'indeterminate' interpretation and potential missed diagnosis, the importance of close collaboration with the reference laboratory, and how serial SRA testing over months can reveal the evolving and ultimately waning nature of aHIT antibodies.

blogs.title: Severe Thrombocytopenia After Cardiac Surgery: Building a Rational Differential
blogs.description: This post uses the case to walk through the systematic evaluation of severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <30×10⁹/L) in the early post-cardiac surgery period. We construct a structured differential diagnosis, including cardiogenic shock-related thrombocytopenia, infection/sepsis, post-transfusion purpura, post-surgical TTP, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, and HIT. For each entity, we highlight key discriminating features—timing of onset, presence of hemolysis, transfusion history, medication timeline, hemodynamic status, and laboratory markers—and demonstrate how each was systematically ruled in or out in this case. We emphasize the importance of not dismissing early severe thrombocytopenia as simply 'post-bypass' and the value of a broad initial workup.

blogs.title: Managing Refractory aHIT: Anticoagulant Sequencing and the Role of IVIG
blogs.description: This post focuses on the management tensions in treating severe autoimmune HIT that does not respond as expected to standard therapy. We examine the decision-making behind the anticoagulant strategy in this case—starting with argatroban for its short half-life and reversibility in the setting of recent stroke and profound thrombocytopenia, then switching to therapeutic-dose fondaparinux due to progressive consumptive coagulopathy and practical ease of administration. We discuss the role of high-dose IVIG in aHIT, why this patient had a blunted response requiring three doses, and the rationale for supplementing antithrombin concentrate before initiating fondaparinux. We also review the use of serial fibrinogen and D-dimer as surrogate markers of HIT-associated hypercoagulability and anticoagulant efficacy.

blogs.title: HIT-Associated Consumptive Coagulopathy: Beyond Thrombosis and Thrombocytopenia
blogs.description: This post examines the underappreciated phenomenon of HIT-associated consumptive coagulopathy, a feature particularly prominent in autoimmune HIT. Using this case, we explore how HIT can produce a secondary consumptive coagulopathy resembling DIC—manifesting as falling fibrinogen, rising D-dimer, and schistocytes on peripheral blood film—despite HIT classically being classified as a prothrombotic, non-consumptive disorder. We discuss the pathophysiology of platelet-mediated thrombin generation, how these laboratory markers can serve as real-time indicators of disease severity and anticoagulant adequacy, and why their presence should raise suspicion for aHIT over classic HIT. We also address the clinical challenge of distinguishing HIT-related schistocytosis from true TTP in the postoperative setting.
